title: NVMe paging QoS and latency amplification lab notes
content:
Purpose:
This note collects experimental runs and quick hypotheses about an operational problem we see in multi-tenant Dedicated hosts: under certain workload mixes the KV cache tail latency spikes by an order of magnitude when host NVMe paging activity increases concurrently with heavy GPU-to-host DMA. The goal is to identify whether NVMe queueing/IOPS/QoS interactions + PCIe contention are amplifying tail latency and triggering excessive eviction churn in the KV layer.

Background / motivation:
- Symptoms: intermittent 95/99/99.9 p50->p99 amplification on token-serving RPCs; correlated with host-level iostat showing sustained NVMe write bursts and elevated nvme latency.
- Suspected causal chain: heavy KV spill/prefetch -> nvme write/read bursts -> nvme queue depth growth -> increased PCIe/host CPU interrupt and DMA contention -> GPU DMA stalls + slower KV fetches -> eviction policy sees increased miss rates and starts more aggressive reclaiming -> extra paging => feedback loop.
- Why it matters: hosted API and Dedicated customers show different failure modes: Dedicated (reserved GPUs) are particularly vulnerable because background eviction/paging is not isolated across tenants.

Experimental environment (lab):
- Hosts: 2-socket AMD Rome, 256GB DRAM, 4 x 3.84TB NVMe (Samsung PM1733), Mellanox ConnectX-6 100Gbps. GPU: 8xA100-40GB on PCIe x16 (no NVLink).
- Kernel: Ubuntu 22.04 + 5.19 with BFQ scheduler, tuned BQL defaults untouched.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime/branch/kv-nvme-probes @ PR 459 (instrumentation: nvme qdepth, per-tenant io counters, pci stall counters).
- Tools: fio (randomrw, mixed), iostat -x, nvme-cli, perf record/stat, nsys for GPU DMA traces, eBPF scripts to capture nvme request latencies per process (simpleprobe).

Microbenchmarks run: (short forms)
1) Baseline knock: single tenant, KV resident 80%, prefetch disabled, small qd fio reads to NVMe -> baseline p50 token latency 1.2ms, p99 3.1ms.
2) NVMe burst: synthetic spill generator (writes 300MB/s sustained, random) + token-serving load -> observed p99 ~ 9.6ms, p99.9 ~ 32ms.
3) GPU DMA concurrency: add simulated GPU inference DMA (nsys trace to show pci bandwidth at 8GB/s) while NVMe burst -> p99 jumped to 18ms, p99.9 > 60ms in worst runs.
4) Isolated NVMe qd sweep: vary fio qdepth 1->64, observe tail increases nonlinearly after qd>=16 when concurrent GPU DMA > 4GB/s.

Key measurements (representative):
- Baseline: p50=1.2ms p95=2.6ms p99=3.1ms
- NVMe-only burst: p50=1.4ms p95=5.8ms p99=9.6ms
- NVMe + GPU DMA: p50=1.8ms p95=12.2ms p99=18.4ms p99.9=62.9ms
- NVMe qd=32 + GPU DMA high: average nvme latency 2.1ms -> tail 40ms+
- Perf summaries: increased softirq time, higher nvme interrupt storms correlated with worst tail windows.

Observations and quick hypotheses:
- NVMe queue depth growth is shifting CPU cycles into processing IO completion and interrupts; the host CPU spends more time in softirq which delays our worker threads that manage KV residency and prefetch completion callbacks.
- PCIe contention is visible: nsys shows GC (GPU) DMA stalls spike during NVMe bursts; the host DMA engine arbitration seems to be favoring NVMe traffic at high QD, causing GPU reads to incur latency.
- Eviction policy (current LRU-ish with adaptive TTL) reacts to slower fetches by lowering the warm threshold and increasing eviction aggressiveness, which compounds misses.
- There is a plausible positive feedback loop: slower NVMe -> slower prefetch completion -> more misses -> more writes (spill) -> more NVMe pressure.

Mitigation experiments tried so far (short notes):
- Rate-limit spillwriter: cap per-tenant NVMe write throughput to 150MB/s (helps p99 by ~30% in mixed tests but increases overall miss rate).
- Lower prefetch parallelism: limit outstanding prefetches per tenant from 64->8 reduces NVMe qd and reduces tail but hurts hit-rate for some workloads.
- Softirq balancing: moved NVMe driver IRQs to isolated cores reduces tail by ~20% in some runs.
- PCIe QoS probe: enabled host-side PCIe traffic shaping (via vendor tools) in a small experiment; preliminary reduction in GPU DMA stalls but not fully resolved.

Open questions / next steps:
- Can we make eviction policy latency-aware instead of purely miss-rate driven? e.g., if disk fetch latency increases, throttle prefetch and avoid panic-evict. Need a small prototype of a latency-aware controller.
- How much does NVMe firmware queueing (internal to device) contribute versus host-side queue depth? Need vendor counters (nvme telemetry) to separate device vs host queueing.
- Should we pursue host-level IO QoS (cgroups/io.max) per-tenant as a short-term control for Dedicated? Pros/cons: coarse but quick.
- Evaluate impact of changing block sizes and synchronous vs async flush patterns on write amplification.

Action items (who/when):
- Diego: instrument nvme telemetry counters (controller queue depth) and add to telemetry dashboard (RINFR-2345) — target 2026-03-07.
- Priya: prototype a latency-aware eviction regulator in the runtime (fast-path: if avg NVMe latency > X ms, reduce prefetch fanout) — spike due 2026-03-14.
- Liam: run vendor-driven PCIe shaping tests on second lab cluster and capture nsys traces — due 2026-03-10.
- Asha: run mixed-tenant replay tests with per-tenant io.max caps and capture overall throughput/latency tradeoffs — schedule 2026-03-09.

Notes-to-self / heuristics observed: 
- qdepth inflection point around 12-16 on our storage (PM1733) when combined with >4GB/s concurrent PCIe traffic. Might shift for other devices.
- Softirq CPU saturation is a good near-term signal; we should alert on that in Console as an early indicator of NVMe-driven tail events.
- Consider exposing a "tenant IO budget" knob in Dedicated config (UI + API) so ops can set IO caps for noisy tenants.

Links and refs:
- fio profiles used: fio-mixed-nvme-qdepth.json (attached in experiment bundle).
- PR with instrumentation: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/459
- Jira: RINFR-2345 (NVMe tail investigation)
- Confluence seed: https://confluence.redwood.ai/pages/NVME-PAGING-QOS

Appendix: quick commands we used
- fio: fio --name=nvme-burst --rw=randrw --bs=128k --size=4G --iodepth=32 --numjobs=4 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1
- nvme top: nvme top /dev/nvme0n1 (vendor telemetry)
- nsys: nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt -o trace1 ./inference-loadgen
- perf top/record around softirq context switching and nvme driver functions

Unresolved: need validation on other host types (Intel, other NVMe models) before we generalize thresholds.

End of notes.
